items.question: Why is this absorption not suitable for all people?
premises: An absorption may arise in this way by contextual association.
Such absorption is possible in principle.
People differ in their tastes and inclinations.
items.inference: Because people have different tastes, this mind-excluding absorption is not suitable for everyone.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of mānasāvarjī as excluding or transcending the mind is slightly compressed in the compound.
items.plain_english: If one objects that such absorption can arise by contextual association, that is possible; but it is not for us, because people have different tastes and this absorption excludes the ordinary mind.

items.question: How does this teaching differ from dualistic teachings about the elements?
premises: In dualistic teachings, the elements and other realities are presented as separated from the supreme Lord.
This teaching is free from duality.
What holds in dualistic systems does not hold in the same way here.
items.inference: In this non-dual teaching, the elements and other realities are not treated as separated from the supreme Lord as they are in dualistic teachings.
uncertainties: dvayavarjite could refer to a doctrine, state, or system; the verse leaves the referent slightly implicit.
items.plain_english: It is said that in dualistic teachings the elements and so on are regarded as separated from the supreme Lord, but in this teaching, which is free from duality, it is not so.

items.question: What is the extent of the unobstructed power of Rudra?
premises: The thirty-sixfold reality is included within this power.
Anything else whatsoever is also included within it.
The great Goddess is identified as Rudra's unobstructed power.
items.inference: The unobstructed power of Rudra, the great Goddess, encompasses the entire thirty-sixfold reality and anything beyond it.
uncertainties: yadanyadapi kiṃcana may gesture beyond the standard thirty-six principles, but its scope is not specified.
items.plain_english: All that is the thirty-sixfold reality, and whatever else there may be, all of that is the great Goddess, the unobstructed power of Rudra.

items.question: Why was the universal nature of earth and other realities expounded earlier?
premises: The unobstructed power of Rudra encompasses all reality.
The second section expounded the universal form of earth and other realities.
That exposition used divisions such as the fifteenfold scheme.
items.inference: Because all reality is pervaded by Rudra's power, the universal form of earth and other realities was rightly expounded in the second section through various divisions.
uncertainties: The exact referent of dvitīye adhikāre depends on the text's internal division and is not fully explicit here.
items.plain_english: For that very reason, in the second section the universal nature of earth and the other realities was expounded through divisions such as the fifteenfold scheme.

items.question: How should partless awareness be understood in the present context?
premises: In the earlier discussion, partless awareness was approached through aspects such as qualities, parts, and wholes.
The same method can be applied in the present case.
The teaching aims at recognition of partless being.
items.inference: Just as partless awareness was understood earlier through differentiated aspects, it should be understood in the same way here.
uncertainties: The compressed compound niraṃśabhāvasaṃbodha may emphasize either realization or conceptual understanding.
items.plain_english: Therefore, just as in the earlier discussion awareness of the partless reality was understood through aspects such as qualities, parts, and wholes, so too it should be understood here.

items.question: By what kinds of properties can the supreme reality be approached?
premises: The supreme reality can be approached through its properties.
These properties include nonconceptuality, firmness, and majesty.
Such properties are forms of power and inhere in the reality itself.
items.inference: Because these properties are inherent power-forms, the supreme reality can be approached through them or through other similar properties.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete on its own and continues into the next verse.
items.plain_english: Therefore, through properties such as nonconceptuality, firmness, and majesty, or through other properties that are inherent power-forms, the reality can be approached.

items.question: How do people worship the supreme Lord through conceptual means?
premises: People may approach the supreme Lord wholly or partially.
Their approach can be shaped by impressions arising from streams of concepts.
These conceptual impressions may be awakened by scripture.
items.inference: Those shaped by scripturally awakened conceptual impressions worship the all-pervading supreme Lord either wholly or partially.
uncertainties: The exact construal of vikalpaughasaṃskārādye is compressed and may admit slight variation in emphasis.
items.plain_english: Thus, those whose mental impressions arise from streams of concepts awakened by scripture worship that all-pervading supreme Lord, either wholly or in part.

items.question: How does conceptual worship lead to resting in the supreme reality?
premises: Worshippers apprehend properties shining within their own concepts.
Skill in those conceptualized properties can mature.
The property-bearer possesses the fullness of all properties.
items.inference: Through skill in the properties appearing within their concepts, worshippers come to rest upon the property-bearer as non-different and full of all properties.
uncertainties: abhedena may indicate identity, non-separation, or non-difference in contemplation; the verse does not force a single technical reading.
items.plain_english: Through their skill in the properties that shine within their own concepts, they come to rest upon the bearer of those properties as non-different and filled with the fullness of all properties.

items.question: Why is conceptual construction said to be necessary for clear experience?
premises: The lord of Śrīvidyā states that sense-born cognition does not objectify the nonconceptual nature.
Conceptual construction is addressed as the means by which inner images are inscribed.
Clear experiences depend on such inwardly inscribed awareness.
items.inference: Although the ultimate nature is nonconceptual, conceptual construction is necessary for experiences to become inwardly articulated and clear.
uncertainties: The verse is a quotation and its metrical breaks make the exact syntactic boundaries slightly compressed.
akṣajā is taken as sense-born cognition, but the quoted context could shade its emphasis.
items.plain_english: For this reason the lord of Śrīvidyā respectfully said: if conceptual construction did not make your nonconceptual nature an object for sense-born cognition, then clear experiences with varied images inscribed within would not arise.

items.question: What scriptural support is cited for this description of the Lord's abode?
premises: The teaching appeals to authoritative texts.
The Śrīmataṅga and related texts describe the Lord's abode with specific qualifications.
One such qualification presents it as consisting of rays of its own power.
items.inference: The Śrīmataṅga and similar scriptures support the view that the Lord's abode is characterized as made of the rays of his own power.
uncertainties: ityādyuktaṃ indicates omitted continuation, so the full scriptural phrasing is not recoverable from this verse alone.
items.plain_english: This is stated in the Śrīmataṅga and other texts, where the abode of the Lord is described, with various qualifications, as consisting of the rays of his own power.

items.question: How is the supreme state described in that divine light?
premises: The scriptural description locates a supreme state in a divine light.
That state is characterized as brilliant, motionless, and unmoving.
It is identified as the supreme, subtle limit whose nature is nectar in all directions.
items.inference: In that divine light there is a brilliant, motionless supreme limit, subtle and nectar-like in all directions.
uncertainties: divi may mean heaven or luminous realm; the verse supports a luminous reading but does not make it explicit.
kāṣṭhā can mean limit, culmination, or direction; culmination fits best here but remains interpretive.
items.plain_english: In that divine light there is a brilliantly radiant, motionless presence with an unmoving form; that alone is the supreme, subtle culmination, whose nature is nectar in all directions.

items.question: Why is this supreme state described as having a form?
premises: The supreme state is beyond coverings, beginning, and end.
It is peaceful, pure, and devoted to reality alone.
Despite this transcendence, it is spoken of as having a form.
items.inference: Although the supreme state transcends ordinary limitations, it is figuratively described as having a form for the sake of expression and contemplation.
uncertainties: upacaryate signals figurative or secondary usage, but the verse does not spell out the pedagogical purpose explicitly.
items.plain_english: With all coverings destroyed, peaceful, intent on reality alone, free from beginning and end, and pure, that state is nevertheless spoken of figuratively as having a form.
